selected.name: Self-referential platform/subreddit meta-humor
selected.instruction: Score 0-10 on how much the joke's comedic content is *about* r/jokes, Reddit, posting, karma, upvotes, or the act of joke-telling itself, rather than about an external topic. 10 = the entire joke is a self-aware commentary on the subreddit/platform or its own reception as a post (e.g., mocking its own upvote prospects, describing addiction to Reddit, complaining about the sub's quality). 0 = no reference whatsoever to Reddit, subreddits, posting, karma, or the joke's own status as a post.
selected.rationale: This is the single clearest recurring pattern among dense_high_card_low items: R12 (Reddit addiction dialogue), R18 (disappointed by r/jokes but keeps reading), R34 ('This joke won't get any upvotes'), R41 (meta joke about not ending jokes), R45 (kleptomaniac spending time on r/jokes), R49 (confessing to a repost), and R52 (commenting instead of posting) are all explicitly about the platform itself. None of the dense_low_card_high items share this trait, suggesting the scorecard bank has no criterion capturing platform-reflexive humor that the dense model rewards.
member_names: Meta-reference to the forum itself with an actual punchline

selected.name: Insider knowledge gate with a self-verifying payoff
selected.instruction: Score the degree to which the joke requires a specific technical, scientific, mathematical or subcultural fact to decode, AND the payoff enacts that fact rather than merely mentioning it. 10 = decoding demands real domain knowledge and the punchline is a live demonstration of the very property invoked (a joke about an unreliable protocol that may not arrive; a number that is literally the square root of another). 5 = domain vocabulary appears but the gag reduces to a generic pun any reader could get. 0 = no specialist knowledge is needed or invoked at any point.
selected.rationale: R08 (UDP, 'you might not get it') sits at dense .987 with card .411, the widest gap in the top band, and R22 (25.8069758 as the root of all evil) at dense .925 / card .274. R17 (ion from dropped electrons, dense .694 / card .030) and R59 (no X and know Y, dense .898 / card .307) repeat the pattern. A scorecard scoring surprise, brevity and wordplay in the abstract will treat these as mild puns; what it misses is the flattery of being the reader who can decode them.
member_names: Insider knowledge gate with a self-verifying payoff
Knowledge gate with payoff proportionate to the gate

selected.name: Dual-Coherence Wordplay
selected.instruction: Score whether a pun or double-meaning produces two fully coherent, self-contained readings of the sentence, each of which makes complete sense in context. A 10 means both meanings are natural, grammatically complete, and contextually appropriate—the reader can genuinely read it either way. A 0 means there is only one natural reading and the second meaning is forced, grammatically broken, or requires ignoring context to work.
selected.rationale: R04 ('laying of hands... blessed') works perfectly as both a church ritual and a literal description. R21 ('make cents/sense') and R53 ('ceiling fans' as honeymoon sight) both have two coherent readings. In contrast, card-favored R31 ('aerials... reception') has misspellings and a strained second meaning, and R01 ('click bait') is a single-layer pun with no dual coherence.
member_names: Both readings of the pivot are fully licensed by the setup

selected.name: Surprise-coherence balance
selected.instruction: Score 10 when the punchline is genuinely unexpected but becomes retrospectively inevitable from the setup; score 0 when it is predictable or feels like an unrelated non sequitur.
selected.rationale: R09 and R16 pair unusual endings with setup clues, whereas the direct pun structure in R10 and R18 offers less of that surprise-to-logic progression.

selected.name: Surprise from withholding the expected punchline
selected.instruction: Score how much the text sets up an obvious punchline and then deliberately refuses to deliver it (or delivers something else), making the refusal itself the joke. 10 = the expected line is clearly implied but withheld; 0 = punchline delivered normally.
selected.rationale: R12 ('But when I do'—never finishes) and R43 ('What's the difference…?' with no answer) derive humor from omission, which a checklist scoring 'has punchline: no' will misread.
member_names: Punchline withheld for the reader to supply
Surprise from withholding the expected punchline

selected.name: Incompleteness: setup with no payoff or pun with no setup
selected.instruction: Score how much the text fails to deliver either a setup or a payoff. 10 = clearly missing one half entirely (truncated or abandoned); 0 = both setup and payoff are present and connected.
selected.rationale: R50 (opens a scene then stops) and R55 (fragment that never forms a joke) are incomplete, which the scorecard may overlook by crediting surface features the dense model treats as fatal.
member_names: Incompleteness: setup with no payoff or pun with no setup

selected.name: Brevity: punchline arrives within ~25 words with no filler
selected.instruction: Score economy: how quickly the text reaches its payoff with no throat-clearing. 10 = complete setup-and-punch in under ~25 words with every word doing work; 0 = rambling or truncated with no payoff.
selected.rationale: R17 ('Muhammed / followers') and R31 ('ion') are extremely short yet land, while R50 and R55 truncate before any payoff—brevity-as-completion distinguishes these.
member_names: Brevity: punchline arrives within ~25 words with no filler

selected.name: Teller as butt, with the admission doing comic work
selected.instruction: Score whether the narrator turns the joke on themselves AND the self-indictment is the payoff rather than a hedge. 10 = the speaker confesses something unflattering about their own habits, taste, or competence, and that confession is the funniest element in the item. 5 = self-deprecation is present but ornamental, an apology attached to a joke that works without it. 0 = no self-reference, or self-reference used purely to pre-excuse weak material.
selected.rationale: R10 confesses to reposting and adds 'I know, I'm a terrible person' as the actual payoff (dense .696 / card .090); R45 asks why it keeps following something it finds disappointing (dense .838 / card .360); R28's explanation of why it never posts is an admission (dense .723 / card .182); R40's 'sorry, this joke has too many layers' folds the apology into the pun (dense .851 / card .311). A scorecard reads these closers as hedging or as commentary outside the joke and discounts them, when they are the joke.
member_names: Teller as butt, with the admission doing comic work

selected.name: No self-explanation or apology attached to the pun
selected.instruction: Score whether the text lets the joke land unassisted. 10 = the punchline is delivered and nothing follows; the reader is trusted to notice. 5 = a brief flourish follows that adds something of its own. 0 = the text announces that a pun has occurred, names the device, or apologizes for the joke's quality.
selected.rationale: Self-labelling is a strong crowd-negative that a craft bank may read as clarity or as an extra beat. R39 (card_pct=0.592, dense_pct=0.056) appends 'That's a play on word'; R42 (card_pct=0.869, dense_pct=0.379) appends 'Click bait.' as a caption on its own gag. R47 apologizes ('sorry, this joke has too many layers') and even there sits far below its dense rank on the scorecard only because the apology itself carries a second pun — the mid-scale case.
member_names: No self-explanation or apology attached to the pun

selected.name: Reference transformation
selected.instruction: Score 10 when a familiar person, text, slogan, or genre is repurposed into a fresh comic mechanism; score 0 when the reference is decorative or simply repeated.
selected.rationale: R06 transforms a political slogan, R19 remixes a biblical naming pattern, and R46 turns a programming concept into a conversational expectation.

selected.name: Wordplay with homophone or near-homophone pivot
selected.instruction: Score how much the humor depends on a word sounding like another word with a different meaning. 10 = the entire joke is built around one homophone the reader must hear; 0 = no phonetic ambiguity is used.
selected.rationale: R36 ('UDP / you might not get it') and R22 ('ATM / cents') rely on a phonetic near-match, which a checklist emphasizing topic or structure may underweight.
member_names: Wordplay with homophone or near-homophone pivot

selected.name: Vivid absurd specificity
selected.instruction: Score 10 when unusual concrete details create a memorable mental image that directly supports the punchline; score 0 when details are generic, decorative, or unrelated to the joke.
selected.rationale: R10, R35, R37, and R59 use a jello-filled cucumber water pistol, layered cupcakes, ceiling fans, or barbecue timing to make otherwise simple premises unusually concrete.

selected.name: Idiom or set-phrase reinterpreted literally
selected.instruction: Score 0-10 on whether the punchline works by taking a common idiom or fixed phrase and reinterpreting it literally in an unexpected context. 10 = the entire joke hinges on a familiar idiom being taken literally. 0 = no idiom is invoked or literalized.
selected.rationale: R21 literalizes 'put it on the record' via an actual turntable needle, and R54 turns the idiomatic filler 'but, f*** it' into a literal 'butt' pun; R13's 'Re:LAX' also plays on 'relax' as a set phrase. All three are dense_low_card_high, pointing to a scorecard preference for idiom-literalization that the dense model underweights relative to other pun types.

selected.name: Concrete image-bearing detail rather than abstract assertion
selected.instruction: Score the specificity of what the reader is asked to picture. 10 = the joke supplies particular, unexpected, physically imaginable detail (a named object, a count, a body, a place) that the payoff then uses. 5 = ordinary concreteness, nothing vivid. 0 = the item is an abstract generality about people or feelings with nothing to picture, or the text has no interpretable referent at all.
selected.rationale: R28 ('Ceiling fans'), R27 ('a waterpistol shaped like a pink cucumber filled with jello', dense_pct=0.587 against card_pct=0.029) and R44 ('365 IDs... free desserts') are dense-high and concrete; R55 supplies the ears and the tattooed list. The abstract end runs the other way: R13 (card_pct=0.970, dense_pct=0.422) and R41 (card_pct=0.583, dense_pct=0.028) offer nothing to see, and R48 has no referent whatsoever yet still outranks its scorecard floor on the dense side.
member_names: Concrete image-bearing detail rather than abstract assertion

selected.name: Taboo transformed
selected.instruction: Score 10 when a dark, political, sexual, or offensive premise is transformed by a specific clever mechanism rather than relying mainly on shock or insult; score 0 when provocation is the entire joke.
selected.rationale: R13, R19, R47, and R56 involve sensitive subjects but differ in how much conceptual reversal or framing supplies the humor.

selected.name: Taboo-register intensity
selected.instruction: Score 0–10 for the extent of sexual, scatological, violent, religiously provocative, death-related, or slur-adjacent material; judge only taboo intensity, never whether its use is effective or funny.
selected.rationale: Taboo register can attract attention or trigger audience reactions independently of craft, while taboo itself may sometimes contribute to genuine humor. The range is visible in R08, R19, R23, R38, R40, and R54.

selected.name: Orthographic noise
selected.instruction: Score 0–10 for spelling errors, grammatical slips, missing capitalization or punctuation, malformed words, run-ons, or unusual spacing; score only the amount of noise, not its quality or humor.
selected.rationale: Editing and submission conditions can leave textual noise that predicts readability and circulation without representing comedic merit. Examples include R15, R17, R35, R56, and R60.

selected.name: Repost/familiarity framing (retelling-chain position)
selected.instruction: Score 0-10 how much the text explicitly signals that the joke or its form has circulated before -- e.g. labeling itself a repost, apologizing for repetition, referencing a joke number/count, or presupposing the audience already knows the joke -- versus presenting itself as newly composed. 0 = no such signal, 10 = the text is primarily framed around its repost/familiarity status. Score only the presence of this framing, not whether the underlying joke is actually stale or fresh.
selected.rationale: R25 ('It seems to me that only reposts make it to the front page nowadays' -- stated twice), R46 ('I bet most of you haven't heard joke #91'), and R47 ('This joke is technically a repost, but I didn't see it anywhere on reddit') all explicitly locate the item within a prior circulation history, a container-position fact distinct from whether this particular telling was voted funny.
member_names: Retelling-chain framing: repost, prior-circulation and numbered-joke tells

selected.name: Sourcing-versus-origination traces in the text
selected.instruction: Score 0-10 for the EXTENT to which the text shows signs of having been transcribed, translated, or lifted from somewhere else rather than composed for this post. Raise the score for: quoted blocks with attribution, citations, or source references; reported-speech framing that credits another teller ('I heard...', 'my friend told me', 'someone said'); dialogue rendered as a transcript with speaker labels or quotation marks; phrasing that reads as translated or non-native in its article, preposition or word-order choices; stand-up cadence or a set-up aside addressed to a live room; formatting residue such as bold or italic markers, asterisks around a title, or a stray URL or domain string. 0 = reads as written on the spot for this post, first-person and unattributed; 10 = explicitly quoted, cited, or transcribed from an external source. Score the provenance trace visible in the text only, and do NOT judge originality, plagiarism, or quality.
selected.rationale: MODE 4 prior handled as a MODE 2 fingerprint: provenance is unseen, but transcription and translation leave characteristic residue, and provenance affects circulation independently of the joke's construction. R03 carries a full quoted scripture block with a chapter-and-verse citation line and curly quotation marks; R43 is a quoted exchange with transcript punctuation and a 'Newly married bride :' speaker label; R28 opens 'I heard this year's Eid...'; R15 has translated-sounding phrasing ('So, once I had that conversation'); R22 has an asterisked title string; R20 contains a bare domain and SEO-spam phrasing. R31, R54 and R59 read as composed in place. Tagged mixed because material that survived being worth transcribing may be genuinely strong.
member_names: Sourcing traces: transcription, translation and lifted-boilerplate fingerprints

selected.name: Template commitment
selected.instruction: Score 0-10 for how much the text follows a conspicuous stock joke scaffold such as a question-and-answer, dialogue labels, numbered steps, or a 'what do you call/because' frame; do not judge whether the feature or joke is good.
selected.rationale: Repeated scaffolds can reveal learned posting habits; practiced format use may also improve construction, making this a mixed nuisance. Examples include R11, R16, and R33.

selected.name: Audience-management furniture: apologies, disclaimers, hedges, requests
selected.instruction: Score 0-10 for the EXTENT of non-joke servicing text addressed to the reader about the post itself: apologies ('sorry'), self-deprecating disclaimers about the poster or the post, pre-emptive predictions about the post's reception, content warnings, tags, edit notes, 'first post' or 'long-time lurker' framing, and any request or anti-request directed at the readership. 0 = the item is entirely joke with no meta-commentary; 10 = a substantial share of the characters are furniture wrapped around the joke. Measure how much of the text is furniture; do NOT judge whether the furniture is endearing or irritating, and do not judge the joke.
selected.rationale: MODE 4. Furniture is textually obvious and separable from the joke body: R29 appends 'I know, I'm a terrible person' to a repost confession, R52 breaks frame with 'sorry, this joke has too many layers', and R27 is nothing but a prediction about its own reception. This is etiquette performance and reader-management, not comic content, so a model that learns furniture is learning a posting convention rather than whether readers laughed. Cited rows: R29, R52, R27.
member_names: Audience-management furniture: apologies, disclaimers, hedges, requests

selected.name: Named topical/political figure or current-event reference
selected.instruction: Score 0-10 the extent to which the item names or clearly identifies a real, contemporaneously salient public figure, politician, or newsworthy event. 0 = no such reference, 10 = the entire joke is built around and requires recognizing the named figure/event. Do not judge whether referencing them is clever or in good taste.
selected.rationale: R10 (Hillary Clinton and Donald Trump), R31 (Ben Carson), R44 (Monica Lewinsky, Bernie, Clinton), and R45 (Trump) all hinge on a specific real-world figure whose salience is a function of when the item was submitted relative to the news cycle, not of the joke's inherent construction.

selected.name: Verbosity and setup-to-punch bulk
selected.instruction: Score 0-10 for the EXTENT of the text's bulk and elaboration, independent of content: total length, number of sentences, amount of scene-setting or narrative build before the final line, presence of dialogue turns, line breaks, paragraph breaks, embedded quotation blocks, enumerated steps or lists. 0 = a single short clause or one-liner under roughly fifteen words; 5 = two to three sentences or a short two-turn exchange; 10 = a multi-paragraph build, extended narrative, or long quoted block. Score length and structural elaboration only. Do NOT judge whether the length is earned, whether the build pays off, or whether brevity is a virtue here.
selected.rationale: Raw length is the classic text-model shortcut and this slice varies by more than an order of magnitude: R03 (long scripture block with paragraph breaks and a citation line), R30 (multi-sentence witch narrative), R56 (labelled BF/Me dialogue with line breaks) and R31 sit at one extreme; R42 ('Macbeth.docx That's a play on word'), R60, R06 and R35 are single clauses. Because both disagreement directions contain both extremes, length can track the disagreement without tracking funniness. Tagged mixed since format length is partly a real craft choice.
